preamble: To mark a golden wedding anniversary

clue.text: Short film screened by badass for those with a supporting role

indicators.note: something screened by another is hidden behind it, so the film sits within the tough soldiers

parts.note: the SAS, Britain's Special Air Service, are the archetypal hard men
a picture, cut short, is a pic

explanation.surface: A tough guy keeps a brief clip hidden, for the benefit of the supporting cast.
explanation.walkthrough: SAS is the Special Air Service, Britain's elite special forces regiment. 'Supporting role' suggests actors, but a spica is a figure-of-eight bandage.
explanation.definitionFit: A spica is a bandage wound in overlapping turns that braces a limb or joint, so these give support.

clue.text: Pru's first amateur theatrical production

indicators.note: the first of Pru's letters is taken, its initial

parts.note: lay means non-professional, as in a lay preacher

explanation.surface: Pru's debut in an amateur dramatic staging.
explanation.definitionFit: A drama staged in a theatre is the usual sense of the word.

clue.text: Make fun of rubbish

definitions.meaning: to tease or banter with someone
husks separated from grain, hence worthless stuff

explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to tease good-humouredly; the noun is husks and refuse, hence anything worthless.

clue.text: She's celebrating gold this weekend: she ___ the previous column

definitions.text: She's celebrating gold this weekend: she ___ the previous column

parts.words: She's celebrating gold this weekend: she ___ the previous column
parts.note: the wife of the golden wedding couple has her name running up the grid column before this one, so she climbs it

explanation.surface: A note about a wife marking her golden wedding and her place in the grid.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap is filled by a verb for climbing: the wife's name reads upward in the column to the left.
explanation.definitionFit: To climb something upward, as a mountaineer climbs a cliff, is the verb that fills the gap.

clue.text: Apply tongue — swallow — spit out bit of war paint

indicators.note: to swallow is to take in, so the licking word takes in the jumbled letters

parts.note: to apply the tongue is to lick

indicators.note: out signals the letters of spit are rearranged, as in put out of order

explanation.surface: A grim sequence of licking, gulping and spitting out a scrap of war paint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swallow' looks like a bird or a gulp; it signals the jumbled letters going inside, after the first two letters. 'War paint' is jokey slang for make-up.
explanation.definitionFit: War paint is jokey slang for make-up, and the coloured stick for lips is one item of it.

clue.text: Maybe Cilla White — or Purple?

indicators.note: maybe suggests a possible version, so the letters of the name are taken in another order

explanation.surface: Wondering whether the singer Cilla is called White or something else.
explanation.walkthrough: Cilla Black was a British singer and TV host; the clue swaps her surname for colours.
explanation.definitionFit: The flowering shrub comes in both white and purple blooms, and its name is also a pale purple shade.

clue.text: Question Othello brought up in drinking chamber

parts.note: to pump someone is to question them hard

indicators.note: in a down light, brought up means the word is written bottom to top

parts.note: Othello is Shakespeare's Moor of Venice

explanation.surface: Othello is interrogated and hauled up in a bar room.
explanation.definitionFit: At spas such as Bath, the hall where visitors went to drink the mineral water had this name.

clue.text: Difficulty with speech as English, say, marry

parts.note: English is an example of a language, or tongue
to tie the knot is to marry

explanation.surface: A speech problem seen as being like English, or perhaps getting married.
explanation.definitionFit: The condition, where a short frenulum restricts the tongue, can impede clear articulation.

clue.text: Irish heading off to penetrate French novelist's old protective garb

indicators.note: to penetrate is to get inside, so the Gaelic letters go into the novelist

parts.note: Colette was the French author of Gigi

indicators.note: heading off means the first letter is removed

parts.note: Erse is the Irish Gaelic language

explanation.surface: A beheaded Irishman somehow piercing a French author's antique armour.
explanation.walkthrough: Erse is the Gaelic language of Ireland; 'heading off' drops its first letter before it goes into the novelist's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A corselet was body armour, and this form names a close-fitting covering for the torso.

clue.text: They are ruined by gin, just like curry!

parts.note: gin is nicknamed mother's ruin, so mothers, or mas, are what it ruins
a la means in the style of

explanation.surface: A boast that gin ruins people, much as a hot curry does.
explanation.walkthrough: Gin's old British nickname is 'mother's ruin', so the things it ruins are mothers: MAS.
explanation.definitionFit: The spice blend gives its name to curried dishes such as tikka versions.

clue.text: Star of the road in 354 days, briefly

indicators.note: in places the road inside the shortened year
briefly means the phrase is cut short, losing its ending

parts.note: a lunar year of twelve moon cycles lasts about 354 days
the M1 is Britain's main north-south motorway, read as MI

explanation.surface: A celebrity of the highway over roughly a year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'briefly' cuts LUNAR YEAR to LUNARY; the M1, Britain's first motorway, goes in as MI.
explanation.definitionFit: A celebrated or eminent person is often called a star, and literally a heavenly light-giver.

clue.text: Some big tops with little jumpers?

definitions.text: Some big tops with little jumpers?

parts.words: Some big tops with little jumpers?
parts.note: big tops are circus tents, and the little jumpers are insects performing tricks rather than knitwear

explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumpers' suggests sweaters; here they are tiny insect performers, and 'big tops' are circus tents.
explanation.definitionFit: Shows of trained parasitic insects were a fairground attraction, a comic miniature of the circus.

clue.text: Attempt spiritual healing with poem about workers

parts.note: a lay is a narrative poem or ballad
on means concerning, as in a talk on art
hands are manual workers, as in farmhands

explanation.surface: A faith healer composing verse about labourers.
explanation.definitionFit: Faith healers place their palms on the sick in the belief that this transmits a cure.

clue.text: Imitate cradling Sybil's head in recess

indicators.note: cradling means holding in the arms, so the mimic word holds the letter

parts.note: to ape is to mimic

indicators.note: the head of Sybil's name is its first letter

explanation.surface: Copying someone while cradling Sybil's head in an alcove.
explanation.definitionFit: The semicircular vaulted end of a church is a recess off the main space.

clue.text: Quiet Muscovite ready to survey surface of steppe? It may be this barren

indicators.note: to survey is to look down over, so in this down light the money sits above the letter

parts.note: sh is the call for silence
ready is slang for cash, and Russian money is in roubles, also spelt rubles

indicators.note: the surface of steppe is its top, the first letter

explanation.surface: A silent Russian with cash looks out over the empty steppe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ready' is British slang for cash; RUBLES sits over the S, 'to survey' it, since the light runs down.
explanation.definitionFit: Treeless grassland lacking bushes is barren in this literal sense.

clue.text: Cued actor, funnily dressed

indicators.note: funnily suggests oddly done, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An actor given his cue turns up in a comic costume.
explanation.definitionFit: Accoutrements are clothes and trappings, so being fitted out in them is being attired.

clue.text: Bill's partner when behaving amorously?

parts.note: lovers are said to bill and murmur like doves, so this word partners bill in that phrase

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name; it is a bird's beak, from the phrase about lovebirds.
explanation.definitionFit: The soft call of a dove completes the idiom for lovers whispering sweet nothings.

clue.text: Precedent for heartless 3 holding book up

indicators.note: holding means containing, so the gutted word wraps around the book
heartless means the central letter is removed

parts.note: 3-down's answer means to tease

indicators.note: in a down light, up means the word is written bottom to top

parts.note: Acts is a book of the New Testament

explanation.surface: A precedent is set when someone holds up a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 3-down means TEASE; 'heartless' drops its middle A to leave TESE, which holds STCA, ACTS turned 'up'.
explanation.definitionFit: A lawsuit whose ruling guides later ones serves as a legal precedent.

clue.text: Got very large eating duck steak

indicators.note: eating means taking inside, so the becoming word swallows the zero

parts.note: got, as in got angry, means turned
a duck in cricket is a score of zero, O
OS is the clothing abbreviation for outsize

explanation.surface: Someone grew enormous by eating duck.
explanation.walkthrough: A cricketer out for zero has made a duck, hence O.
explanation.definitionFit: A small round cut from the fillet of beef is a classic French dish.

clue.text: He's celebrating gold this weekend: he goes ___ in the row above

definitions.text: He's celebrating gold this weekend: he goes ___ in the row above

parts.words: He's celebrating gold this weekend: he goes ___ in the row above
parts.note: the husband of the golden wedding couple has his name written right to left in the row above, heading toward sunset

explanation.surface: A note about a husband marking his golden wedding and his place in the grid.
explanation.walkthrough: The husband's name reads leftward in the row above, the compass direction of left on a map.
explanation.definitionFit: On a map left is the direction of sunset, so a name read leftward travels that way.

clue.text: Ridiculous sale, epic — 50% off!

indicators.note: ridiculous suggests something absurd, so the letters are put in a nonsensical order
50% of epic is its first half

explanation.surface: A ridiculous sale on an epic offers half price.
explanation.walkthrough: '50%' takes EP, half of EPIC, to join SALE in the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: One who has dropped off or nodded off is in slumber.

clue.text: See 24
Golden wedding celebration, for example — partial to platinum anniversary?

indicators.note: partial means only in part, so the number loses its outer letters

parts.note: a platinum anniversary marks seventy years

explanation.surface: Asking whether a couple at their golden wedding favour reaching their platinum one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'partial to' looks like fondness; it means part of SEVENTY, the platinum year, minus S and Y.
explanation.definitionFit: A party marking fifty years is an occasion, an example of the general noun.

clue.text: Dispute using weapon, first to last

indicators.note: first to last means the opening letter moves to the end

parts.note: a sword is a bladed weapon

explanation.surface: Settling an argument by drawing a weapon first.
explanation.definitionFit: To have words with someone is to quarrel, so the plural noun means an argument.

clue.text: Play that we blush at, right? We both did it on TV

indicators.note: to play with letters is to toy with them, so the words that follow are rearranged

explanation.surface: A saucy stage farce that makes the couple blush, and which they performed for television.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play' looks like the definition but is the anagram signal; the definition is the closing words, since Timothy West and Prunella Scales starred in a BBC2 version of Joe Orton's farce in 1987.
explanation.definitionFit: The golden wedding couple, both actors, appeared together in a 1987 television production of this Orton comedy.

clue.text: Young Parisian, one of fashion

parts.note: a Parisian says un for one and de for of
the rage is the current fashion

explanation.surface: A youthful Parisian is one of the fashionable set.
explanation.definitionFit: Being below the legal age for something means being too youthful for it.

clue.text: This corny Shakespearean solver's coarse

parts.note: an ear is the grain-bearing part of a corn plant
thy is the old form of your, addressing the solver

explanation.surface: A solver's verdict that this Shakespearean corn is rather vulgar.
explanation.definitionFit: Earthy humour is crude or bawdy, unrefined like soil.

clue.text: It's shambolic when American with muscle checks in (it's my view)

indicators.note: to check in is to enter, so the pair go inside the jumbled letters
shambolic means chaotic, so the letters are disordered

parts.note: pec is short for pectoral muscle

explanation.surface: A chaotic hotel scene when a muscular American checks in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shambolic' rearranges the letters of It's to IST, and 'checks in' puts the American and the muscle between its S and T. The definition is the bracketed aside.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying one suspects something is offering a personal opinion or guess.

clue.text: Money once placed in green shade

indicators.note: in tells us the placed word goes inside the colour

parts.note: pea green is a shade of green
set means put down or placed

explanation.surface: Cash was formerly hidden in a green-tinted spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Spain's former currency was replaced by the euro in 2002.
